In brief

Parody. "The last farewell was affecting in the extreme [...] my old mashtub what's waiting for me down Limehouse way": nothing in Ulysses is more hilarious than this longest of the Cyclops parodies, three paragraphs of execution reportage parroting the Citizen's patriotic blather about "the brothers Sheares and Wolfe Tone beyond on Arbour Hill and Robert Emmet and die for your country." Rather than aping supposed medieval grandeur as most of the previous parodies have done, this one adopts the fulsome style of a contemporary newspaper article gushily covering a high-society event. Newspapers were associated with complacent patriotic bloviating in Aeolus, and that bombastic vein is tapped again here, but now the soaring style struggles to beautify repulsive subject matter and suffers vertiginous tonal drops. The Irish cult of heroic martyrdom does not appear to good advantage.

At more length

The scene in the parody seems more or less present-day, but the execution is inspired by historical events, most notably the young Robert Emmet's 1803 execution for high treason. This century-old event has been resonating in the novel for three chapters. In Wandering Rocks Tom Kernan looks eastward to where James's Street becomes Thomas Street and thinks, "Down there Emmet was hanged, drawn and quartered. Greasy black rope. Dogs licking the blood off the street when the lord lieutenant's wife drove by in her noddy." Much of Sirens is devoted to the bar patrons' relishing of the similar story told in "The Croppy Boy." At the end of that chapter Bloom gazes on a poster commemorating Emmet's noble speech from the dock and then deflates its heroism with a loud fart. Cyclops perpetuates both the highminded tone (the hero is happy to die for his country, adoring crowds throng gaily to the spectacle) and its bathetic undermining (visiting dignitaries are criminals, police circulate through the crowd ready to break heads, a devoted fiancée is ludicrously inconstant).

Emmet's college friend Thomas Moore celebrated his memory in several stirring songs, but for the first half of the 19th century his cause of armed rebellion was condemned both by unionist authorities and by Daniel O'Connell. In mid-century, however, Young Irelanders and Fenians revived his reputation, and by the turn of the 20th century he had become a secular saint in the eyes of Irish nationalists. Immortalized by Moore's "She is far from the land," his engagement to Sarah Curran made him not only a martyr to the cause of Irish independence but also a paragon of romantic love.

Joyce unquestionably centered his parody on this idealized figure, but he probably also intended to evoke other brave young Irishmen who had chosen death over subjugation. The Citizen mentions three members of the United Irishmen rebellion of 1798, also executed by the British authorities: John and Henry Sheares, and Wolfe Tone. Early nationalist readers of Ulysses would no doubt have thought of still more revered heroes, including perhaps the Invincibles hanged in 1883 for the Phoenix Park murders, or the leaders of the 1916 Easter Rising.

Joyce's spectacle draws an "assembled multitude which numbered at the lowest computation five hundred thousand persons"—described later as "That monster audience." The number is clearly meant to sound hyperbolic, but it does not too greatly exaggerate the numbers reported to have attended O'Connell's "monster meetings" in the early 1840s. This bizarre conflation of a public execution with a political rally is perhaps not completely absurd, given the way some executions had been treated (at least in 18th century London) as festive public spectacles. But it is made completely absurd by the inclusion of a viewing stand of visiting foreign dignitaries, "quick excursion trains and upholstered charabancs" to import fans from the countryside, musical entertainments, a world-famous executioner greeted with the cheers normally reserved for athletic heroes, a splendid final meal, a romantic reunion of lovers, and a dramatic resolution of the problem of a lost fiancé.

Joyce's mockery of newspaper writing scales new heights of purple prose: "The deafening claps of thunder and the dazzling flashes of lightning which lit up the ghastly scene testified that the artillery of heaven had lent its supernatural pomp to the already gruesome spectacle"; "Quietly, unassumingly, Rumbold stepped on to the scaffold in faultless morning dress and wearing his favourite flower, the Gladiolus Cruentus. He announced his presence by that gentle Rumboldian cough which so many have tried (unsuccessfully) to imitate—short, painstaking yet withal so characteristic of the man"; "he, with an abnegation rare in these our times, rose nobly to the occasion"; "The nec and non plus ultra of emotion were reached when the blushing bride elect burst her way through the serried ranks of the bystanders and flung herself upon the muscular bosom of him who was about to be launched into eternity for her sake."

These noble sentiments are regularly subverted by lapses into low tones: riotously off-color suggestions in the foreign delegates' names (Putrid Pest, KissAssOnly, Penisinbath-Ballsvalley), grotesque disembowelling details ("a terra cotta saucepan for the reception of the duodenum, colon, blind intestine and appendix etc when successfully extracted and two commodious milkjugs destined to receive the most precious blood of the most precious victim"), madcap comedy ("It was exactly seventeen o'clock"), leering sexual obscenity ("Encouraged by this use of her christian name she kissed passionately all the various suitable areas of his person which the decencies of prison garb permitted her ardour to reach"), ignoble Cockney speech ("God blimey if she aint a clinker, that there bleeding tart. Blimey it makes me kind of bleeding cry, straight, it does, when I sees her cause I thinks of my old mashtub what's waiting for me down Limehouse way").

The Irish Literary Revival and the Gaelic Revival gave way, not inevitably perhaps but seamlessly, to Sinn Fein and the Easter Rising. In retrospect, the glorification of all things Irish proved perfectly compatible, for better and for worse, with an embrace of militant nationalism. Writing Cyclops in 1919, Joyce cast a cold eye not only on the reverence for ancient Celtic myths but also on the hagiography of heroic martyrdom. His pacifistic protagonist registers one response to political violence: "But it's no use, says he. Force, hatred, history, all that. That's not life for men and women, insult and hatred." The mocking send-up of Emmet-worship expresses a similar intent.

Gifford suggests that this long passage "owes a debt of parody to Washington Irving's (1783-1859) story 'The Broken Heart', in The Sketch Book (1819-20)." Irving's story is about the devastating effect that Emmet's death had on his fiancée. He does describe Emmet in admiring tones similar to those employed in Joyce's passage: "Every one must recollect the tragical story of young E——, the Irish patriot; it was too touching to be soon forgotten. During the troubles in Ireland, he was tried, condemned, and executed, on a charge of treason. His fate made a deep impression on public sympathy. He was so young—so intelligent—so generous—so brave—so every thing that we are apt to like in a young man. His conduct under trial, too, was so lofty and intrepid. The noble indignation with which he repelled the charge of treason against his country—the eloquent vindication of his name—and his pathetic appeal to posterity, in the hopeless hour of condemnation,—all these entered deeply into every generous bosom, and even his enemies lamented the stern policy that dictated his execution." Joyce's treatment of Sarah Curran, however, bears no resemblance whatsoever to the picture of blighted romantic love that Irving paints.

John Hunt 2026
